caption:
Goldman Sachs has limited Claude Code and GitHub's AI coding tools to its roughly 12,000 engineers.
Most traders and bankers who had been building their own tools with them lost access in October.
The bank says it tests tools first, then keeps them with the people best suited to use them.

Should AI coding tools be for engineers only?

paragraphs.text: Goldman Sachs has restricted Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub coding tools to its engineering staff, cutting off most of the traders and bankers who had been using them. The change came through updated internal guidance in October that was first reported by Bloomberg in early November 2026, according to Gadget Review, Startup Fortune and FStech.

About 12,000 Goldman engineers keep full access to the tools. One group outside engineering is also exempt: the bank's strats, employees whose jobs combine trading, quantitative research and software engineering.
How traders were using the tools

Before the change, staff across the business had used the coding agents for several months. According to the reports, traders used them to monitor client trading flows, to model possible market moves and position changes, and to produce written and visual material. Some described an idea in plain language and got a rough prototype that engineers could later build out, a practice widely known as vibe coding.
FStech reported that the restriction has frustrated some traders who had built the tools into their daily routines.

The move is a turn from the bank's public tone earlier in 2026. In July, Chief Information Officer Marco Argenti praised vibe coding by traders and bankers, saying the bank's engineers could then refine what they produced. Argenti also told CNBC that agentic coding tools could make a strong developer 30 to 40 percent more productive, according to Startup Fortune.

Goldman spokesperson Nick Carcaterra described the change as part of a normal process rather than a reversal. He said the firm makes certain AI tools available to find the best use cases across the firm and, after a period of experimentation, puts them with the people best placed to use them over the long term. The findings of that evaluation have not been made public, and Gadget Review noted that the exact cause of the restriction has not been confirmed.

The reports point to productivity and risk management as the concerns behind the review, including how code written by agents is reviewed, how data is handled and who is accountable in a regulated business. Goldman's own in-house AI assistant, which combines models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Alphabet, reportedly remains broadly available across the firm.

It is not the first limit Goldman has placed on Claude. In late April, the bank cut off Claude access for its staff in Hong Kong, which Bloomberg linked to a strict reading of its contract with Anthropic, since Anthropic does not offer its models in Greater China. Startup Fortune reported that JPMorgan later pulled Claude access for its Hong Kong employees as well. In August, Goldman partner Chris Churchman warned that heavy reliance on AI could weaken the analytical skills of future bankers, FStech reported, citing Quartz.

The decision shows a large bank separating two kinds of AI use. Chat assistants stay open to everyone, while agents that write and run code are kept with staff whose work already goes through engineering review. For employees outside engineering, the experiment with building their own tools has ended for now at one of Wall Street's most visible AI adopters.
Watch whether other large banks follow Goldman in limiting coding agents to engineers, and whether Goldman publishes what its evaluation of trader and banker use actually found.
